name: Supply and Demand
teaser: The most fundamental force in economics: when something is scarce and wanted, its price rises; when it's abundant and ignored, its price falls. This single mechanism coordinates the decisions of billions of strangers.

exploreAction.targetName: The logic of supply and demand
exploreAction.instruction: Read a clear explanation of how supply and demand curves interact to set prices, then find one real-world example where a supply shock changed prices overnight.

name: The Invisible Hand
teaser: Adam Smith's metaphor for how individuals pursuing their own self-interest inadvertently benefit society. A baker doesn't make bread out of charity — but you eat because he profits.

exploreAction.targetName: Adam Smith's original passage on the invisible hand
exploreAction.instruction: Find Smith's actual words in The Wealth of Nations (Book IV, Chapter II) and note how modern economists interpret — and misinterpret — the metaphor.

name: Opportunity Cost
teaser: The value of the next best alternative you give up when making a choice. Every decision has a hidden price tag — not what you pay, but what you sacrifice.

exploreAction.instruction: Think of three decisions you made this week. For each, identify the opportunity cost — what you gave up — and consider whether the trade was worth it.

name: Comparative Advantage
teaser: Even if you're better at everything than someone else, you both benefit from specializing. Trade isn't about who's best — it's about who gives up the least to produce.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a clear exposition of Ricardo's England-Portugal cloth-wine example, then explain why the principle still holds even when one country is more efficient at everything.

name: Gross Domestic Product
teaser: GDP sums the market value of every final good and service produced in a country in a year. It's the most widely used scorecard for economies — and one of the most misunderstood.

exploreAction.targetName: How GDP is calculated and what it misses
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the three methods of calculating GDP (production, income, expenditure), then name two important things GDP fails to measure.

name: Inflation
teaser: When prices rise across the economy, each unit of currency buys less. Moderate inflation is normal; runaway inflation destroys savings and trust in money itself.

exploreAction.targetName: What causes inflation and why it matters
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation, then look up the current inflation rate in your country and what's driving it.

name: Interest Rates
teaser: The price of borrowing money. Central banks raise rates to cool inflation and lower them to刺激 growth — making this the most powerful lever in macroeconomic policy.

exploreAction.targetName: How interest rates shape the economy
exploreAction.instruction: Understand how the Federal Reserve's federal funds rate ripples through mortgages, savings accounts, and business investment, then check today's rate.

name: Commodities
teaser: Wheat, oil, copper, gold — things that are identical no matter who produces them. Commodity prices are the raw pulse of the global economy, reacting to weather, wars, and demand in real time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between spot and futures markets for commodities, then check the current price of crude oil and what's moving it.

name: Trade Deficit
teaser: When a country imports more than it exports, the gap is a trade deficit. It's not inherently bad — it can mean consumers are thriving — but it reveals structural dependencies.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the US has run persistent trade deficits for decades without economic collapse, and why the deficit number alone doesn't tell the full story.

name: Fiscal Policy
teaser: Government spending and taxation as tools to steer the economy. Cut taxes and spend more to stimulate; raise taxes and cut spending to cool down. Simple in theory, brutal in practice.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare Keynesian and austerity approaches to fiscal policy, then look at one real-world example where fiscal stimulus succeeded or failed.

name: Monetary Policy
teaser: Central banks control the money supply and interest rates to manage inflation and employment. It's the unseen hand that moves markets while most people never notice.

exploreAction.targetName: How central banks use monetary policy
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the three main tools of monetary policy (open market operations, discount rate, reserve requirements), then explain why inflation targeting became the dominant framework.

name: Quantitative Easing
teaser: When interest rates hit zero, central banks buy bonds to inject money directly into the economy. It's emergency medicine for the financial system — powerful, controversial, and hard to reverse.

exploreAction.targetName: How QE works and its consequences
exploreAction.instruction: Understand how the Fed's QE programs after 2008 and 2020 expanded the balance sheet, then discuss whether QE primarily helped asset owners or the broader economy.

name: John Maynard Keynes
teaser: The economist who argued that governments must spend during downturns to prevent spiraling unemployment. His ideas reshaped how the world manages recessions — and his name became a political label.

exploreAction.targetName: Keynes's core argument in The General Theory
exploreAction.instruction: Read a summary of Keynes's central insight — that aggregate demand drives employment, not just supply — and consider why governments still debate his ideas 90 years later.

name: Adam Smith
teaser: The Scottish moral philosopher who wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776), arguing that free markets, division of labor, and self-regulating competition create prosperity. Often called the father of economics.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapter of The Wealth of Nations
exploreAction.instruction: Read Smith's famous pin factory example about division of labor, then note how modern assembly lines and software development embody the same principle.

name: Milton Friedman
teaser: The monetarist who argued that inflation is always a monetary phenomenon — too much money chasing too few goods. His free-market ideas influenced Reagan and Thatcher.

exploreAction.instruction: Understand Friedman's claim that controlling the money supply is the key to controlling inflation, then compare his view with Keynesian fiscal stimulus.

name: Thomas Piketty
teaser: The French economist whose book Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) used 200 years of data to argue that capitalism naturally concentrates wealth unless governments intervene.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn Piketty's famous r > g formula (returns on capital exceed economic growth), then consider what policies could counteract wealth concentration.

name: Game Theory
teaser: The mathematics of strategic decision-making: when your outcome depends on what others do, how do you choose? Prisoner's dilemma, Nash equilibrium, and the logic of cooperation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the prisoner's dilemma and Nash equilibrium, then find a real-world example where strategic interdependence shaped an economic outcome.

name: Behavioral Economics
teaser: People aren't rational calculators. We're biased, emotional, and predictably irrational. Behavioral economics studies how psychology distorts economic decisions — and how to design around it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about loss aversion, anchoring, and the endowment effect, then notice one of these biases in your own recent spending decisions.

name: Externalities
teaser: When a factory pollutes, the cost falls on everyone nearby — not just the buyer. Externalities are the costs or benefits that markets ignore, and they're why markets sometimes fail.

exploreAction.instruction: Understand how pollution is a negative externality and education is a positive one, then explain why carbon taxes try to 'internalize' the externality.

name: Gini Coefficient
teaser: A number between 0 and 1 measuring how unequally income is distributed. Zero means everyone earns the same; one means one person has everything. Most countries fall between 0.25 and 0.60.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Gini coefficient is calculated from the Lorenz curve, then compare the Gini values of three countries with very different economic systems.

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
teaser: Money you've already spent shouldn't influence your next decision — but it does. We keep watching bad movies because we paid for the ticket, and finish bad meals because we ordered them.

exploreAction.targetName: The sunk cost fallacy in everyday life
exploreAction.instruction: Identify a time you kept investing in something just because you'd already invested, then explain why a rational decision-maker would ignore sunk costs.

name: Price Discrimination
teaser: Charging different prices to different people for the same product. Student discounts, airline tickets, and happy hours are all forms of extracting more value from different willingness to pay.

exploreAction.targetName: First, second, and third-degree price discrimination
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the three degrees of price discrimination and find one real example of each in your daily life.

name: Capitalism
teaser: An economic system where private individuals own the means of production and prices are set by markets. In practice, every capitalist economy is a hybrid — the debate is how much government belongs in the mix.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare laissez-faire capitalism, social democracy, and state capitalism, then identify which model best describes the country you live in.

name: Socialism
teaser: An economic system where the means of production are owned collectively — by the state, workers, or communities. The goal is equitable distribution; the challenge is coordination without markets.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between democratic socialism and authoritarian socialism, then examine one country where socialist policies coexist with market economies.

name: Central Banks
teaser: The Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan — institutions that control interest rates, print money, and serve as lenders of last resort. They steer economies without elections.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the mandate of the Federal Reserve (dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices), then compare it with the ECB's single mandate of price stability.

name: Globalization
teaser: The increasing interconnectedness of economies through trade, investment, and technology. It lifted hundreds of millions from poverty — and hollowed out manufacturing in developed nations.

exploreAction.instruction: Trace the three waves of globalization (1870–1914, 1945–1980, 1990–present), then identify which benefits and costs you personally experience from global trade.

name: Command Economy
teaser: When the government owns everything and makes all production decisions. The Soviet Union, Maoist China, and North Korea tried it. The results were shortages, stagnation, and eventual collapse or reform.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the 'calculation problem' — why central planners can't efficiently allocate resources without market prices — and find one historical example of its consequences.

name: Mercantilism
teaser: The pre-industrial belief that a nation's wealth is measured in gold and silver. Governments restricted imports and boosted exports to accumulate precious metals — an obsession that fueled colonial empires.

exploreAction.targetName: Mercantilism and the age of empires
exploreAction.instruction: Understand how mercantilist policies drove European colonialism, then explain why Adam Smith argued against mercantilism in favor of free trade.

name: Labor Theory of Value
teaser: The idea that a good's value comes from the labor needed to produce it. Ricardo proposed it; Marx used it to argue that workers are exploited. Neoclassical economics replaced it with marginal utility.

exploreAction.targetName: From Ricardo to Marx: the labor theory of value
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the labor theory of value evolved from classical economics to Marx's critique of capitalism, then explain why marginalism eventually displaced it.

name: Marginal Utility
teaser: The satisfaction from one more unit of something. The first sip of water on a hot day is priceless; the tenth is worthless. This diminishing satisfaction explains why demand curves slope downward.

exploreAction.targetName: The law of diminishing marginal utility
exploreAction.instruction: Understand why the fifth slice of pizza brings less joy than the first, and how this principle explains pricing strategies like 'buy two, get one free.'

name: Elasticity
teaser: How sensitive is demand to a price change? Insulin is inelastic — diabetics pay whatever they can. Netflix is elastic — raise the price, subscribers leave. Elasticity determines who has pricing power.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how elasticity is calculated and why it matters for pricing, then compare the elasticity of gasoline versus restaurant meals.

name: Monopoly
teaser: When one firm controls the entire market, it can set prices without fear of competition. Monopolies are efficient for the producer and terrible for the consumer — which is why antitrust law exists.

exploreAction.targetName: How monopolies form and why they're regulated
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the sources of monopoly power (economies of scale, network effects, patents, regulation), then find one modern monopoly or near-monopoly and its impact on consumers.

name: Oligopoly
teaser: A market dominated by a few large firms — airlines, telecoms, auto manufacturers. Each firm's decisions depend on what rivals do, creating a strategic dance of price wars and collusion.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how oligopolies differ from perfect competition and monopoly, then identify an oligopoly you interact with regularly and how it affects your choices.

name: Perfect Competition
teaser: A theoretical market where无数 small firms sell identical products, nobody can influence prices, and profits are driven to zero. No real market is perfect — but it's the benchmark everything else is measured against.

exploreAction.targetName: The assumptions and implications of perfect competition
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the four conditions for perfect competition (many buyers/sellers, identical products, free entry/exit, perfect information), then explain why no real market meets all four.

name: Creative Destruction
teaser: Joseph Schumpeter's idea that capitalism advances by destroying the old to make way for the new. The buggy whip maker died so the automobile could live. Progress is built on ruins.

exploreAction.instruction: Understand how innovation destroys existing industries while creating new ones, then name three industries that were 'creatively destroyed' in your lifetime.

name: The Great Depression
teaser: The 1929–1939 economic catastrophe: US GDP fell 30%, unemployment hit 25%, and banks collapsed by the thousands. It reshaped economics, government, and the relationship between the two.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the chain of events from the 1929 crash to the banking panics, then explain how Friedman argued the Fed's failure to act made the depression worse.

name: The 2008 Financial Crisis
teaser: Subprime mortgages, CDOs, and a global banking collapse. The crisis destroyed $2 trillion in economic activity, reshaped regulation, and left a generation skeptical of financial institutions.

exploreAction.targetName: The Big Short (2015) or a documentary on the crisis
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening hour of The Big Short or a documentary, then explain how mortgage-backed securities turned housing defaults into a global financial meltdown.

name: Stagflation
teaser: The nightmare scenario: prices rise while the economy stagnates and unemployment climbs. The 1970s oil shocks proved that inflation and recession could happen simultaneously — breaking Keynesian orthodoxy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks triggered stagflation, then explain why this combination of problems was so difficult for traditional economic policy to address.

name: Hyperinflation
teaser: When inflation exceeds 50% per month, money becomes worthless. Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe, Venezuela — people carry wheelbarrows of cash for bread. It destroys savings, trust, and social fabric.

exploreAction.instruction: Read about the Weimar Republic's hyperinflation (1923) or Zimbabwe's (2008), then explain what governments did to eventually restore monetary stability.

name: The European Union
teaser: A political and economic union of 27 countries that share a single market, a common regulatory framework, and (for 20 of them) a single currency. The most ambitious experiment in economic integration ever attempted.

exploreAction.targetName: How the EU single market works
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the four freedoms of the EU single market (goods, services, capital, people), then consider how Brexit tested whether a country can leave a deeply integrated market.

name: Bretton Woods
teaser: In 1944, 44 nations met in New Hampshire to design the post-war economic order: fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar, which was tied to gold. The system collapsed in 1971 but its institutions endure.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bretton Woods system and its legacy
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Bretton Woods agreement created the IMF and World Bank, then explain what happened when Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility in 1971.

name: Demographic Dividend
teaser: When a country's working-age population grows faster than dependents, economic growth accelerates. East Asia's miracle was partly demographic — but the window closes as populations age.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Japan, South Korea, and China each experienced a demographic dividend, then consider what happens when that window closes.

name: Dutch Disease
teaser: When a resource boom makes your currency stronger, killing your manufacturing exports. The Netherlands discovered this with natural gas in the 1960s — and many oil-rich nations have repeated the pattern.

exploreAction.targetName: The resource curse and Dutch Disease
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a natural resource boom can paradoxically harm an economy, then find a modern example of a country suffering from Dutch Disease.

name: Middle-Income Trap
teaser: Countries that grow rapidly from poverty to middle income often stall there. The low-wage advantage fades, but innovation hasn't yet taken hold. Getting rich is easier than staying rich.

exploreAction.targetName: Why some countries escape the middle-income trap
exploreAction.instruction: Compare South Korea's escape (innovation, education) with Argentina's stagnation, then identify what policies distinguish countries that break through from those that don't.

name: Tragedy of the Commons
teaser: When shared resources are free to use, individuals overconsume until the resource is destroyed. Overfishing, traffic congestion, and climate change are all commons problems in disguise.

exploreAction.targetName: The tragedy of the commons and solutions
exploreAction.instruction: Understand Garrett Hardin's argument, then explore three solutions (privatization, regulation, community management) with real-world examples of each.

name: Asymmetric Information
teaser: When one side of a deal knows more than the other, markets break down. Used car sellers know more than buyers; doctors know more than patients. This explains why trust, regulation, and signaling matter.

exploreAction.instruction: Read about George Akerlof's 'Market for Lemons' paper, then find a modern example where asymmetric information creates market problems (healthcare, used cars, or online shopping).

name: Transaction Costs
teaser: The hidden costs of doing business: searching for partners, negotiating contracts, enforcing agreements. Ronald Coase argued that firms exist precisely to reduce these frictions.

exploreAction.targetName: Coase and the nature of the firm
exploreAction.instruction: Understand why Coase believed firms exist to minimize transaction costs, then explain why some activities happen inside firms while others happen in markets.

name: Public Goods
teaser: Street lights, national defense, clean air — things everyone benefits from but nobody wants to pay for individually. Free-riders let others foot the bill, so public goods are almost always underprovided by markets.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the two properties of public goods (non-excludable and non-rivalrous), then explain why private companies rarely build lighthouses.

name: The Arsenal of Democracy
teaser: During WWII, the US transformed its civilian economy into a military production machine. Factories that made cars now made tanks. GDP doubled. It proved that government-directed spending could reshape an economy overnight.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the US economy shifted from civilian to military production between 1941 and 1943, then consider what this tells us about the limits of peacetime industrial policy.

name: Planned Obsolescence
teaser: Deliberately designing products to fail or become outdated. Lightbulb manufacturers once conspired to limit bulb lifespan. Today, software updates and fashion cycles do the same job more subtly.

exploreAction.targetName: The history and ethics of planned obsolescence
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the Phoebus cartel (lightbulb manufacturers), then identify a modern product where planned obsolescence is suspected and its economic consequences.

name: Universal Basic Income
teaser: A regular cash payment to every citizen, no strings attached. Advocates say it eliminates poverty traps and empowers individuals; critics worry about cost, work incentives, and inflation.

exploreAction.targetName: The case for and against UBI
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about UBI experiments in Finland, Kenya, and Stockton, then weigh the evidence on whether guaranteed income reduces poverty without killing work incentives.

name: The Renminbi and China's Rise
teaser: China's currency went from worthless to a global reserve currency contender. The country's economic rise — from agrarian poverty to the world's second-largest economy in 40 years — is the greatest growth story in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Deng Xiaoping's reforms in 1978 unleashed China's growth, then consider whether the country's state-capitalist model can sustain growth as it ages.

name: Debt-to-GDP Ratio
teaser: A country's total government debt divided by its annual economic output. Japan's ratio exceeds 260% — yet it borrows at near-zero interest. The ratio matters, but context matters more.

exploreAction.targetName: How to interpret sovereign debt levels
exploreAction.instruction: Compare the debt-to-GDP ratios of Japan, the US, and Greece, then explain why similar ratios can mean very different things depending on who borrows and in what currency.

name: Venture Capital
teaser: The fuel of innovation: investors bet on unproven startups hoping one will become the next Google. Most fail; the winners pay for everything. It's high-risk, high-reward capitalism at its most concentrated.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the VC funding stages (seed, Series A/B/C) and the power law distribution of returns, then explain why VCs push for exponential growth rather than steady profits.

name: Hedge Funds
teaser: Private investment funds that use aggressive strategies — short selling, leverage, derivatives — to generate returns. They charge high fees, are mostly unregulated, and serve only wealthy investors.

exploreAction.targetName: What hedge funds do and why they matter
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between hedge funds and mutual funds, then find a famous hedge fund strategy (long/short, macro, arbitrage) and one notable success or failure.

name: Cryptocurrency Economics
teaser: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and thousands of tokens: a parallel financial system built on cryptography and decentralization. Some see digital gold; others see speculative mania. The economics are genuinely novel.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Bitcoin's fixed supply (21 million), halving schedule, and proof-of-work create digital scarcity, then debate whether this makes it money, gold, or speculation.

name: Scarcity
teaser: The foundational problem of economics: resources are finite, but wants are infinite. Every economic system — capitalism, socialism, communism — is ultimately a way of managing scarcity.

exploreAction.targetName: Why scarcity is the root of economics
exploreAction.instruction: Understand how scarcity forces trade-offs at every level — personal, corporate, national — then consider whether technology could ever eliminate scarcity.

name: Economic Efficiency
teaser: A state where resources are allocated so no one can be made better off without making someone worse off (Pareto efficiency). Beautiful in theory; ruthlessly indifferent to fairness in practice.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the Pareto criterion, then explain why a perfectly efficient outcome can still be deeply unequal — and why economists debate whether efficiency or equity should come first.

name: Sole Proprietorship
teaser: The simplest business form: one person, unlimited liability, total control. More Americans are sole proprietors than any other business type — freelancers, consultants, food truck owners, and creators.

exploreAction.instruction: Understand the advantages (simplicity, control) and disadvantages (unlimited liability, difficulty raising capital) of sole proprietorships compared to LLCs or corporations.

name: Monopsony
teaser: When there's only one buyer in a market, they can squeeze suppliers. Most people know about monopoly; monopsony is its overlooked twin — and it shapes labor markets more than you'd think.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a dominant employer in a small town can suppress wages below competitive levels, then find evidence of monopsony in modern labor markets.

name: The Golden Age of Capitalism
teaser: From 1945 to 1973, the Western world experienced unprecedented growth, falling inequality, and rising wages. High taxes, strong unions, and regulated finance created a broadly shared prosperity.

exploreAction.targetName: What made the postwar boom possible
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the conditions that enabled the Golden Age (Bretton Woods, Marshall Plan, strong unions, Keynesian policy), then debate whether those conditions can be recreated.

name: The Neoliberal Turn
teaser: In the 1980s, Reagan and Thatcher dismantled postwar economic consensus: deregulated markets, privatized industries, weakened unions, and cut taxes. It reshaped the global economy for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the core policies of the neoliberal turn (tax cuts, deregulation, privatization), then evaluate what it delivered — and what it cost.

name: BRICS
teaser: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa — and now a dozen more. A bloc of developing nations challenging Western economic dominance. Whether they're a real alternative or a photo opportunity remains unclear.

exploreAction.targetName: BRICS and the shift in global economic power
exploreAction.instruction: Learn why BRICS nations want alternatives to the dollar-dominated financial system, then assess whether the bloc can translate economic size into geopolitical influence.

name: The Asian Financial Crisis
teaser: In 1997, a currency collapse in Thailand cascaded across Asia. Currencies plummeted, banks failed, and the IMF prescribed austerity that deepened the pain. It redrew the map of global finance.

exploreAction.instruction: Trace the contagion from Thailand's baht to Indonesia, Korea, and beyond, then evaluate whether the IMF's austerity prescriptions helped or hurt.

name: The Future of Work
teaser: Automation, AI, remote work, and the gig economy are transforming employment. The question isn't whether jobs will change — it's whether workers will be ready when they do.

exploreAction.targetName: How technology is reshaping labor markets
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the gig economy, AI displacement, and remote work trends, then consider which jobs are most vulnerable and which are most resilient to automation.

name: Shareholder Primacy
teaser: The doctrine that a corporation's sole purpose is to maximize shareholder value. Milton Friedman made it gospel. The Business Roundtable's 2019 reversal suggested the era may be ending.

exploreAction.targetName: The rise and fall of shareholder primacy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Friedman's 1970 argument that corporate social responsibility is 'fundamentally subversive,' then explain why 181 CEOs reversed course in 2019.

name: Economic Growth Theory
teaser: Why do some countries grow rich while others stay poor? Growth theory tries to answer: Solow's model says capital accumulation matters; endogenous growth theory says ideas and institutions matter more.

exploreAction.targetName: Solow growth model vs endogenous growth
exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Solow's model predicts convergence that never happens, then explain how Romer's endogenous growth theory makes ideas the engine of prosperity.

name: Economic Freedom
teaser: How free are people to trade, own property, start businesses, and keep their earnings? Indices like the Heritage Foundation's rank countries — but the link between freedom and prosperity is more nuanced than it appears.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how economic freedom indices are constructed (property rights, trade openness, regulatory burden), then examine whether high economic freedom always correlates with prosperity.

name: Deindustrialization
teaser: When factories close and manufacturing jobs vanish from developed nations. The Rust Belt in America, the Midlands in Britain — entire communities hollowed out as production moves overseas.

exploreAction.targetName: The causes and consequences of deindustrialization
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how automation and offshoring together eliminated manufacturing jobs in developed nations, then consider what policies could help displaced workers.

name: Negative Interest Rates
teaser: When central banks push rates below zero, savers pay for the privilege of keeping money in the bank. Japan, Europe, and Switzerland tried it — a radical experiment in desperate economic times.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn which central banks used negative rates and why, then discuss whether they stimulated lending or just punished savers.

name: Modern Monetary Theory
teaser: MMT argues that governments issuing their own currency can never 'run out of money' — the only real constraint is inflation. It's radical, controversial, and gaining influence in policy circles.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn MMT's key insight (sovereign currency issuers face real resource constraints, not financial ones), then compare its predictions with what happened during COVID-era spending.

name: Privatization
teaser: Selling state-owned enterprises to private owners. In theory, private management is more efficient. In practice, privatization has produced both triumphs (British Telecom) and disasters (Russian oligarchs).

exploreAction.targetName: The wave of privatizations in the 1980s–90s
exploreAction.instruction: Compare successful privatizations (UK telecommunications) with failed ones (Russian energy sector), then identify what conditions make privatization work or fail.

name: Economic Sanctions
teaser: When nations use trade restrictions as weapons. Sanctions can cripple economies — but they also hurt ordinary people and often fail to change the behavior of authoritarian regimes.

exploreAction.instruction: Study the track record of sanctions (Cuba, Iran, Russia), then debate whether they achieve political goals or primarily inflict humanitarian suffering.

name: The Creative Economy
teaser: Industries built on intellectual property and human creativity — film, music, design, gaming, software. The creative economy generates trillions globally and is increasingly where young people want to work.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why creative industries have unusual economics (high fixed costs, near-zero marginal costs, winner-take-all markets), then identify a creative industry trend reshaping your world.

name: The Philippine Economic Story
teaser: Once the second-richest country in Asia after Japan, the Philippines fell behind its neighbors through decades of misrule, crony capitalism, and population growth. Its diaspora became its greatest export.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Philippines went from postwar prosperity to relative decline, then examine how overseas remittances became a lifeline for the economy.

name: Regressive vs Progressive Taxation
teaser: A regressive tax hits the poor harder (sales tax, VAT). A progressive tax hits the rich harder (income tax, capital gains). The balance between them shapes inequality and public services.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between progressive, proportional, and regressive taxes, then find which type dominates your country's tax system and its effect on inequality.

name: Exchange Rates
teaser: The price of one currency in terms of another. Exchange rates affect everything from your vacation budget to national trade balances. They're set by markets, central banks, and geopolitics simultaneously.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between floating and fixed exchange rates, then check today's USD/EUR rate and what's driving it.

name: The Stock Market
teaser: Where companies sell ownership stakes and investors bet on the future. The stock market is not the economy — but it's the economy's most visible scoreboard, reflecting greed, fear, and expectation in real time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the basics of stock exchanges, P/E ratios, and market indices, then check the S&P 500's year-to-date performance and what's driving it.

name: Economic Bubbles
teaser: When asset prices detach from fundamental value and everyone buys because prices are rising. Tulips in 1637, dot-com in 2000, housing in 2008 — the pattern repeats because human psychology doesn't change.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the five stages of a bubble (displacement, boom, euphoria, profit-taking, panic), then compare the dot-com bubble with the 2008 housing bubble.

name: Paradox of Thrift
teaser: Saving is good for you — but if everyone saves at once, spending collapses, businesses fail, and everyone gets poorer. Keynes's counterintuitive insight that personal virtue can be collective vice.

exploreAction.targetName: Why saving too much can harm the economy
exploreAction.instruction: Understand the paradox of thrift through a simple example, then explain why it matters during recessions when consumer confidence collapses.

name: The Fisher Effect
teaser: Irving Fisher's elegant equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation. When inflation rises, interest rates rise too — the real cost of borrowing stays constant.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fisher equation and its implications
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the Fisher equation, then explain why the Fed raises rates when inflation rises — and why savers aren't actually better off when nominal rates track inflation.

name: Stakeholder Capitalism
teaser: The idea that corporations should serve workers, communities, and the environment — not just shareholders. It's making a comeback as trust in pure profit-maximization fades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the stakeholder theory proposed by R. Edward Freeman, then evaluate whether companies can genuinely serve multiple stakeholders or if trade-offs make it impossible.

name: Remittance Economies
teaser: Over 200 million migrants send money home — $656 billion in 2022. For the Philippines, Mexico, and dozens of other nations, remittances are a lifeline that keeps families afloat and economies running.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the scale and impact of global remittances, then examine whether remittance-dependent economies become trapped in a cycle of labor export.

name: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
teaser: A company with no CEO, no board, no headquarters — just code and token-based voting. DAOs are experiments in radical decentralization. Some govern billions; most collapse in chaos.

exploreAction.targetName: How DAOs work and what they govern
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how DAOs use smart contracts and token voting to make collective decisions, then examine one successful DAO and one that failed spectacularly.

name: The Philippine Overseas Worker Program
teaser: Since the 1970s, the Philippines has actively exported labor: nurses to the Gulf, seafarers worldwide, domestic workers to Hong Kong. It's both a success story and a structural dependency.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Philippine government institutionalized labor migration, then discuss the social costs of a policy that treats human capital as the country's main export.

name: Absolute Advantage
teaser: When one country can produce more of a good with the same resources than another. It's simpler than comparative advantage — but it's the starting point for understanding why trade works.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between absolute advantage (who produces more) and comparative advantage (who sacrifices less), then explain why comparative advantage matters more for trade.

name: Deflation
teaser: When prices fall across the economy. Sounds great for consumers — but deflation makes debts harder to repay, delays purchases (why buy today if it's cheaper tomorrow?), and can spiral into depression.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the deflationary spiral (falling prices → delayed spending → lower output → more unemployment → more deflation), then examine Japan's lost decades as a case study.

name: Neoliberalism
teaser: The economic philosophy that free markets, deregulation, privatization, and minimal government intervention maximize prosperity. Dominant from the 1980s to 2008 — now facing serious critique.

exploreAction.targetName: The rise and critique of neoliberalism
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the core tenets of neoliberalism (Washington Consensus), then evaluate its track record: what it delivered and what it failed to deliver.

name: The Gig Economy
teaser: Uber, DoorDash, Fiverr — work fragmented into short-term tasks with no benefits, no job security, and algorithmic management. It's flexibility for some and precarity for others.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how gig platforms use algorithms to manage workers, then debate whether gig workers are independent entrepreneurs or misclassified employees.

name: The Fiscal Multiplier
teaser: When the government spends a dollar, does the economy grow by more or less than a dollar? The multiplier is Keynesian economics' most important — and most debated — number.

exploreAction.targetName: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier
exploreAction.instruction: Learn why multipliers vary (higher in recessions, lower at full employment), then find an estimate of the multiplier for infrastructure spending vs tax cuts.

name: Fiat Currency
teaser: Money backed by nothing but government decree. The dollar, euro, and yen have no intrinsic value — they work because people trust the institutions behind them. Trust is the only collateral.

exploreAction.targetName: How fiat money differs from commodity money
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between fiat money (government decree) and commodity money (gold-backed), then explain why the world abandoned the gold standard.

name: The Philippine BPO Boom
teaser: Call centers, back-office processing, IT outsourcing — the Philippines became the world's second-largest BPO destination after India. It created millions of jobs and reshaped the urban middle class.

exploreAction.targetName: How the BPO industry transformed the Philippines
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how English proficiency and time zone alignment gave the Philippines a BPO advantage, then examine the social costs of night-shift service work.

name: Leading Economic Indicators
teaser: Stock markets, building permits, consumer confidence — numbers that predict where the economy is heading. Economists build composite indices from these signals, but the economy always surprises.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the yield curve inversion, PMI, and initial jobless claims as recession predictors, then check the current state of two leading indicators.

name: The Philippine Peso Story
teaser: From Spanish colonial silver to American-era pesos to the 1997 Asian crisis crash — the Philippine peso's history mirrors the country's turbulent journey through colonialism, dictatorship, and democracy.

exploreAction.instruction: Trace the peso from Spanish colonial times through American influence to modern floating exchange rates, then explain how currency crises reflect deeper economic vulnerabilities.

name: Poverty Traps
teaser: When being poor makes it harder to stop being poor. Low income → no education → low productivity → low income. Breaking the cycle requires intervention — but what kind works?

exploreAction.targetName: How poverty traps work and how to break them
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the mechanisms that trap people in poverty (credit constraints, health shocks, educational gaps), then examine one successful anti-poverty program and why it worked.

name: The Invisible Hand (Smith, 1776)
teaser: Adam Smith's metaphor: self-interested individuals accidentally serve the public good through markets. It's the foundation of capitalism — but Smith also warned about monopolies and inequality.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Invisible Hand (Smith, 1776) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Keynesian Economics (1936)
teaser: John Maynard Keynes argued governments should spend during recessions to stimulate demand. His General Theory created macroeconomics and justified the New Deal. Austrians still disagree.

name: GDP as a Measure (1934)

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of GDP as a Measure (1934) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Tragedy of the Commons (1968)

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Tragedy of the Commons (1968) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Game Theory in Economics — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Federal Reserve (1913) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Laffer Curve (1974) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Supply and Demand (Ricardo, 1817)
teaser: David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage and supply-demand equilibrium became economics' core framework. Prices emerge from scarcity and willingness to pay — no central planner needed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Supply and Demand (Ricardo, 1817) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Gold Standard (1870s-1971) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

teaser: Milton Friedman argued inflation is always a monetary phenomenon — too much money chasing too few goods. His influence shaped central banking for decades, until 2008 proved velocity of money matters.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Monetarism (Friedman, 1960s) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Great Depression (1929-39) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

teaser: How much does quantity demanded change when price changes? Insulin has low elasticity — diabetics must buy it. Jewelry has high elasticity — consumers can skip it. Elasticity shapes pricing strategy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Elasticity of Demand — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Opportunity Cost (Ricardo, 1817)
teaser: The value of the next best alternative you gave up. Every choice has an opportunity cost — attending college costs 4 years of salary. It's the most fundamental concept in economics.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Opportunity Cost (Ricardo, 1817) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Efficiency Wage Theory
teaser: Paying above market rate motivates workers, reduces turnover, and attracts talent. Henry Ford's $5/day wage (double the average) cut turnover from 370% to 16%. Higher wages can be cheaper.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Efficiency Wage Theory — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Dutch Tulip Mania (1637)
teaser: Tulip bulbs traded for the price of houses — then the market crashed overnight. The first recorded speculative bubble showed how human psychology drives markets to irrational extremes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Dutch Tulip Mania (1637) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Comparative Advantage (Ricardo, 1817)
teaser: Even if Country A is better at everything, both countries benefit from trade if each specializes in what they're relatively best at. Ricardo's insight is why free trade generally increases total wealth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Comparative Advantage (Ricardo, 1817) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Veblen Good
teaser: Luxury goods that sell more as price rises — Hermès bags, Patek Philippe watches. Thorstein Veblen called it 'conspicuous consumption.' The price IS the product — it signals status.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Veblen Good — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Phillips Curve (1958)
teaser: Inflation and unemployment have an inverse relationship — lower unemployment means higher inflation. A.W. Phillips drew the curve from 100 years of UK data. The 1970s stagflation broke it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Phillips Curve (1958) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Paradox of Thrift (Keynes, 1936)
teaser: If everyone saves more during a recession, total spending falls and the recession worsens. Individual virtue becomes collective vice. It's why austerity during downturns can backfire.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Paradox of Thrift (Keynes, 1936) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Schumpeter's Creative Destruction (1942)
teaser: Joseph Schumpeter argued capitalism advances through destroying old industries. The horse cart gave way to the automobile, the fax to email. Innovation requires bankruptcy of the outdated.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Schumpeter's Creative Destruction (1942) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Circular Flow of Income
teaser: Households spend, firms earn, workers earn, households spend again. The circular flow model shows how money moves through an economy — and how leaks (savings, taxes, imports) reduce activity.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Circular Flow of Income — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Utility Maximization
teaser: Consumers allocate spending to maximize satisfaction given budget constraints. The marginal utility per dollar should equal across all goods. It's the microeconomic foundation of consumer choice.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Utility Maximization — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Coase Theorem (1960)
teaser: If property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are low, parties will negotiate efficient outcomes regardless of who holds initial rights. Ronald Coase's insight reshaped law and economics.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Coase Theorem (1960) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Kuznets Curve
teaser: Income inequality rises then falls as economies develop — an inverted U-shape. Simon Kuznets observed it in US data. Critics argue it's not inevitable — policy choices matter more than development stage.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Kuznets Curve — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: The Solow Growth Model (1956)
teaser: Robert Solow showed long-run growth comes from technological progress, not capital accumulation. His model explains why poor countries can catch up — but only if they adopt better technology.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of The Solow Growth Model (1956) — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Gig Economy
teaser: A labor market characterized by short-term, flexible jobs rather than permanent positions. Uber, DoorDash, and Fiverr exemplify the model. 36% of US workers participate in gig work. It offers flexibility but often lacks benefits and job security.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Gig Economy — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Universal Basic Income
teaser: A government program providing all citizens with a regular unconditional cash payment. Finland's 2017-2018 trial with 2,000 unemployed people found recipients were happier and healthier with no reduction in employment. Alaska's Permanent Fund has paid dividends since 1982.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Universal Basic Income — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Modern Monetary Theory
teaser: An economic theory suggesting governments that issue their own currency cannot run out of money and should spend to achieve full employment. Critics warn of inflation risks. It gained attention during COVID-19 when governments spent trillions without apparent consequence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Modern Monetary Theory — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Behavioral Economics
teaser: The field combining psychology and economics to understand why people make irrational financial decisions. Richard Thaler won the 2017 Nobel Prize for this work. Nudges like automatic enrollment in retirement savings increased participation from 49% to 86%.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Behavioral Economics — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Shadow Banking
teaser: Non-bank financial intermediaries that provide services similar to banks but operate outside regular banking regulations. The shadow banking system reached $63 trillion globally in 2019. It played a major role in the 2008 financial crisis through mortgage-backed securities.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Shadow Banking — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Dutch Disease
teaser: An economic phenomenon where a country's natural resource boom leads to currency appreciation that hurts other export sectors. The Netherlands experienced it after finding natural gas in 1959. Nigeria's oil boom devastated its agricultural sector in the 1970s.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Dutch Disease — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Gini Coefficient
teaser: A measure of income inequality ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). South Africa has the highest at 0.63 while Scandinavian countries average 0.25. The US Gini coefficient rose from 0.39 in 1967 to 0.49 in 2021.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Gini Coefficient — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Trickle-Down Economics
teaser: The theory that tax cuts for corporations and the wealthy stimulate economic growth benefiting everyone. Empirical evidence is mixed — the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced corporate tax from 35% to 21% but primarily boosted stock buybacks over wages.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Trickle-Down Economics — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Pareto Efficiency
teaser: An economic state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. Vilfredo Pareto observed that 80% of Italy's land was owned by 20% of the population in 1896. The 80/20 rule appears throughout economics and business.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Pareto Efficiency — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Stagflation
teaser: A toxic combination of stagnant economic growth, high unemployment, and rising inflation. The US experienced it from 1973-1982, triggered by oil shocks. Paul Volcker, Federal Reserve chair, ended it by raising interest rates to 20% in 1981.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Stagflation — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Externalities
teaser: Costs or benefits of an economic activity that affect third parties not involved in the transaction. Pollution is a negative externality — factories impose health costs on communities. Carbon taxes attempt to internalize climate change costs.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Externalities — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Creative Destruction
teaser: Joseph Schumpeter's 1942 concept describing how innovation constantly replaces old industries. The automobile destroyed horse-drawn carriages, streaming killed Blockbuster, and smartphones eliminated cameras and GPS devices. It drives long-term economic progress.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Creative Destruction — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Veblen Goods
teaser: Luxury products for which demand increases as the price rises because they signal status. Hermès Birkin bags and Rolls-Royce cars follow this pattern. Thorstein Veblen coined 'conspicuous consumption' in 1899 to describe status-seeking spending.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Veblen Goods — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Fiscal Cliff
teaser: A situation where automatic tax increases and spending cuts occur simultaneously, potentially causing economic contraction. The US faced one in 2012-2013 when Bush-era tax cuts expired alongside sequestration. Congress eventually passed a partial compromise.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Fiscal Cliff — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: K-Shaped Recovery
teaser: An economic recovery where different segments of society recover at different rates, diverging over time. After COVID-19, tech companies and stock owners boomed while service workers struggled. The top 10% of earners saw wealth increase 25% during the pandemic.

name: Supply Chain Economics
teaser: The network of organizations involved in producing and distributing goods. COVID-19 exposed vulnerabilities — a single semiconductor shortage affected auto, electronics, and appliance industries. The cost of shipping a container from China to the US rose 10x in 2021.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Supply Chain Economics — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Carbon Pricing

name: Crypto Economics

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Crypto Economics — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Inclusive Growth

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Inclusive Growth — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Debt-to-GDP Ratio
teaser: A country's total debt relative to its economic output, indicating its ability to repay. Japan's ratio exceeds 260% — the highest in the world — yet it avoids crisis because most debt is held domestically. The US ratio reached 123% in 2023.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Debt-to-GDP Ratio — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Petty Cash Float
teaser: A small amount of currency kept on hand for minor expenses. A typical office maintains $100-$300 in petty cash for supplies, postage, and incidentals. Companies reconcile petty cash monthly, requiring receipts for every disbursement.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Petty Cash Float — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Revenue Recognition
teaser: Accounting principles determining when a company records income. ASC 606 requires recognizing revenue when performance obligations are met. Amazon recognizes cloud revenue monthly but retail revenue at delivery — a key difference in how earnings appear.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Revenue Recognition — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Goodwill in Accounting
teaser: The premium paid for an acquiring company above its net asset value. When Microsoft bought LinkedIn for $26.2 billion in 2016, most of the premium was recorded as goodwill. If goodwill becomes impaired, companies must write down its value, hitting profits.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Goodwill in Accounting — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Monopsony
teaser: A market with only one buyer, giving it outsized power over sellers. Amazon dominates book purchasing, affecting publisher prices. Labor monopsony occurs when a single employer controls a local job market, depressing wages below competitive levels.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Monopsony — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Velocity of Money
teaser: The rate at which money changes hands in an economy. When velocity drops, it signals economic weakness even if money supply grows. US velocity fell from 2.0 in 1999 to 1.1 in 2023, explaining why massive money printing didn't cause immediate inflation.

name: Hedge Funds

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Hedge Funds — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Moral Hazard
teaser: When someone takes greater risks because they know someone else bears the cost. Bank bailouts encourage reckless lending — 'too big to fail.' AIG's 2008 bailout cost $182 billion partly because its London division took excessive risks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Moral Hazard — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Crony Capitalism

name: Dynamic Pricing

exploreAction.instruction: Read one thorough overview of Dynamic Pricing — pay attention to what makes it worth knowing, then try explaining its most surprising detail to someone else in under a minute.

name: Platform Economics

name: Zipf's Law
teaser: The empirical observation that the second most frequent item occurs about half as often as the most frequent, the third about a third as much, and so on. It applies to city populations, word frequencies, and income distributions. It emerges from preferential attachment.

name: Tragedy of the Commons

name: Efficient Market Hypothesis

name: Keynesian Economics

name: Colonial Economics
teaser: Economic systems imposed during European colonialism that extracted resources from colonies. Belgium's exploitation of Congo's rubber reduced its population by half. Colonial-era trade patterns persist — former colonies still export raw materials to former colonizers.

name: Positive Economics
teaser: Economic analysis based on facts and cause-effect relationships, separate from value judgments. 'Raising minimum wage increases unemployment' is a positive statement testable with data. It contrasts with normative economics, which involves value-based recommendations.

name: Economic Indicators
teaser: Statistics like GDP, unemployment rate, and CPI that signal economic health. The Conference Board's Leading Economic Index predicts recessions 6-9 months ahead. The yield curve inversion has predicted every recession since 1955 with only one false signal.

name: Financial Literacy
teaser: Knowledge of financial concepts like compound interest, inflation, and diversification. Only 57% of American adults are financially literate according to the FINRA Foundation. Financial education programs show modest but real improvements in savings behavior.

name: Public Goods
teaser: Goods that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous — everyone benefits regardless of payment. National defense, streetlights, and clean air are public goods. Free-rider problems make private markets underprovide them, justifying government provision through taxation.

name: Information Asymmetry
teaser: When one party in a transaction has more information than the other. Used car sellers know more than buyers — George Akerlof's 'Market for Lemons' (1970) showed this can collapse markets. Insurance companies' advantage over applicants drives medical underwriting.

name: Sweat Equity
teaser: Non-monetary investment of time and effort into a business or project. Startup founders accept lower salaries hoping equity will appreciate. In real estate, home improvements that increase value without cash investment are sweat equity. Mark Zuckerberg turned down $1 billion for Facebook.

name: External Debt
teaser: Money a country owes to foreign creditors. Sri Lanka's 2022 default on $51 billion in external debt triggered economic collapse. Greece's debt crisis in 2010 exceeded 130% of GDP, requiring three bailout programs totaling €289 billion.

name: Cost-Benefit Analysis
teaser: A systematic approach to evaluating decisions by comparing total costs against total benefits. The US EPA estimates the Clean Air Act benefits at $2 trillion annually against $65 billion in compliance costs — a 30:1 return. It's required for major federal regulations.
